children: The first full week of October, though light, brings a diverse earnings slate spanning consumer staples, beverages, travel, apparel, and AI infrastructure, with companies offering fresh reads on both consumer demand and the capital-intensive technology buildout. PepsiCo
will provide insight into spending patterns across food, beverages, and apparel, while Delta Air Lines
offers a key read on travel demand and airline economics.
On the technology side, Applied Digital
remains a notable AI infrastructure name as data center expansion and power availability continue to shape the sector, while Penguin Solutions
adds exposure to enterprise technology and memory solutions. Saratoga Investment
rounds out the slate with a financial-services angle, making for a week that spans consumer resilience, travel demand, and the ongoing investment cycle in AI infrastructure.
Below is a rundown of major quarterly updates anticipated in the week of October 5 to October 9:
The week starts off relatively quiet, as there are no major earnings announcements planned.

, the U.S. importer and marketer of Corona, Modelo Especial, and Pacifico, is set to report its fiscal Q2 FY2027 results after Tuesday’s close, with the stock near a 52-week low as investors assess whether beer volumes can return to sustained growth.

In Q1 FY2027, Constellation delivered a beat, with EPS of $3.43 versus $3.27 consensus and net sales of $2.43B versus $2.42B expected. Beer depletions returned to positive territory at 0.6% after three consecutive quarters of declines, while beer operating margin held at 38%. Management raised its full-year FY2027 GAAP EPS guidance and maintained comparable EPS guidance of $11.20 to $11.90. However, core brands remained under pressure, with Modelo Especial depletions down 2% and Corona Extra down 5%. CEO Nick Fink attributed softness among the company's core Hispanic consumer base partly to immigration-related job and spending concerns.

A key positive for margins came from the U.S. government's decision to exclude malt-based beer from the scope of Section 232 aluminum tariffs, removing an estimated $58M annual cost headwind. However, management struck a more cautious tone on beer volumes at the Barclays Global Consumer Conference in September, contributing to a sharp pullback in the shares. JPMorgan lowered its price target to $133 from $165 while maintaining Neutral, while TD Cowen, Evercore ISI, BNP Paribas, and Barclays also reduced targets. The stock has fallen sharply in recent weeks and remains close to its 52-week low of $113.34.
Constellation has beaten EPS estimates in 6 of the past 8 quarters, exceeding revenue estimates in 5 of those reports.

, the denim and lifestyle apparel brand, is set to report fiscal Q3 2026 results after Wednesday’s close, with the company continuing its DTC-first transformation even as the stock has pulled back about 18% over the past 90 days.

In Q2 FY2026, Levi reported net revenue of $1.56B, up 8% Y/Y, while adjusted EPS of $0.28 beat the $0.24 consensus. Adjusted EBIT margin expanded to 9.0%, and DTC accounted for 52% of total net revenue. Beyond Yoga revenue increased 23% Y/Y, while Europe delivered 24% reported revenue growth. Management raised full-year FY2026 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, lifting reported net revenue growth to 7.0%-7.5% from 5.5%-6.5% and adjusted diluted EPS to $1.46-$1.52 from $1.42-$1.48.

For Q3, management expects revenue growth of 4%-5% and adjusted EPS of $0.34-$0.36. Recent analyst actions have focused on tariffs and cotton costs, with UBS maintaining a Buy and $34 price target while highlighting potential EPS upside if tariff rates remain below expectations. Jefferies lowered its target to $25 from $27, and Stifel to $27 from $28, both retaining Buy ratings, while Wells Fargo moved to Equal-Weight. The quarter should provide another read on whether Levi's can sustain its growth trajectory while navigating tariff and input-cost pressures.
Levi has beaten EPS estimates in each of its last 8 quarters and revenue estimates 6 times in that span.

, the global food and beverage company behind Lay’s, Doritos, Pepsi, Gatorade, and Quaker, is set to report Q3 2026 results before Thursday’s open, with North American volume pressure increasingly colliding with a renewed push for pricing.

In Q2 2026, PepsiCo reported revenue of $24.18B, up 6.4% Y/Y, while core EPS rose 4% to $2.20, narrowly missing the $2.21 consensus. North American food volume was flat and beverage volume declined 4%, while international operations delivered stronger growth. Management maintained its full-year fiscal 2026 outlook for low-to-mid-single-digit organic revenue growth.

The pricing strategy has since shifted. PepsiCo plans to raise prices on select brands including Doritos and Ruffles, along with certain beverages and dips, by low-to-mid-single-digit percentages later this year or early next year, reversing price cuts of as much as 15% introduced earlier in 2026. The move comes as the company faces weaker North American volumes and higher costs for ingredients, packaging, logistics, and fuel. JPMorgan recently downgraded the stock to Neutral and cut its price target to $138, while other analysts have also reduced targets amid concerns over North American sales and the salty snacks business.
PepsiCo has beaten EPS and revenue estimates in 6 of its last 8 quarters.

, the Atlanta-based premium U.S. carrier, is set to report Q3 2026 results before Friday’s open, with the quarter expected to reflect continued strong travel demand alongside higher fuel costs and a growing competitive focus on in-flight connectivity.

In Q2 2026, Delta reported record revenue of $19.76B, up 18.7% Y/Y, while adjusted EPS of $1.56 beat the $1.47 consensus. The airline reported a 9% operating margin and maintained its full-year adjusted EPS guidance of $6.50-$7.50 and free-cash-flow outlook of $3B-$4B. Premium and loyalty revenue grew at a mid-teens rate, while American Express remuneration increased 10% to more than $2B.

A high-profile dispute over Delta’s in-flight Wi-Fi strategy has added noise heading into the quarter. Delta has chosen Amazon’s LEO satellite network for its next-generation connectivity rather than SpaceX’s Starlink, with the LEO rollout planned for 2028. Recent reports said CEO Ed Bastian criticized working with Elon Musk, prompting Musk to publicly criticize Delta and its leadership; the reported comments attributed to Bastian have not been independently confirmed by Delta. Meanwhile, competitors including United are expanding Starlink connectivity, keeping the issue in focus as Delta continues to rely on existing providers ahead of the Amazon rollout.
Delta has beaten revenue estimates in 8 straight quarters, missing EPS expectations just once in that time frame.
